card.stem: A house in the vernacular tradition, as shown in the sketch, was built over 100 years ago without insulation and is now in need of significant refurbishment. The occupants have decided to refurbish the house on a step-by-step basis over a number of years.
card.questionText: A survey of the house reveals: external random rubble stone walls, 450 mm in thickness, with an internal and external lime render; traditional cut roof with natural slates; suspended timber ground floor. Select any two of the above areas and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps involved in upgrading each area selected. Show how the refurbishment should be carried out in a manner that respects the character of the original house and ensures the reuse of materials.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed areas, each note 6 and sketch 6 = 12. External random rubble wall: keep the wall breathable with no vapour barriers; hempcrete, wood fibre boards or lime plasters inside or out; a French drain against rising damp; layers progressively more permeable towards the outside. Traditional cut roof: minimal intervention: slates numbered, stored and reused; impermeable felt replaced with a vapour-diffuse membrane; only decayed parts of rafters spliced or replaced in the same timber; hygroscopic insulation such as sheep’s wool and wood fibre board; counter battens for ventilation. Suspended timber ground floor: floorboards numbered and lifted; sub-floor ventilation checked; decayed joists or boards replaced; insulation between the joists on netting or battens with a breather membrane; boards and skirting relaid as labelled.
The refurbishment respects the character of the original house, such as matching materials, profiles and the original roof plane.
Materials reused, such as numbered slates and floorboards relaid and decayed timber replaced only where needed.

card.questionText:
Using the following data, calculate the U-value of the insulated concrete ground floor: Concrete floor slab thickness 125 mm; Extruded polystyrene insulation thickness 200 mm; Damp proof membrane (DPM) thickness 0.30 mm; Sand blinding thickness 30 mm; Hardcore thickness 225 mm.
Thermal data of floor: Resistance of top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Conductivity of concrete (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of polystyrene insulation (k) 0.031 W/m °C; Conductivity of damp proof membrane (DPM) (k) 0.450 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.260 W/m °C.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity, thickness and resistance.

rows.verbatim: Insulated concrete ground floor (9 points × 3 marks)
rows.contextNote: Six resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k: top surface 0.1040 (given); slab 0.125/0.160 = 0.7813; insulation 0.200/0.031 = 6.4516; DPM 0.00030/0.450 = 0.0006; sand blinding 0.030/0.160 = 0.1875; hardcore 0.225/1.260 = 0.1786. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance, the sum of R = 7.70 m²°C/W.
U = 1/Rt = 1 ÷ 7.7 = 0.1298 W/m²K (1 mark for the formula).

card.questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in the design of a Passive House: building form; indoor air quality; foundation design.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of orientation in the siting of a Passive House. Show the sun path in your sketch.

(c) A Passive House, as shown in the sketch, may overheat in summer. Discuss two reasons why overheating occurs and, using notes and freehand sketches, show two design details that would reduce the possibility of overheating.

rows.verbatim: Design of a passive house - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each note 5 and sketch 5 = 10. Building form: a simple, compact form with a surface-to-volume ratio of 0.7 or less: less material, easier to heat and make airtight; complex forms add wall area, cold bridges and wind chill. Indoor air quality: build tight and ventilate right: MHRV supplying filtered fresh air and extracting moist air from wet rooms; at most 0.6 air changes per hour; humidity 30–60%; CO₂ below 1000 ppm. Foundation Design: an insulated foundation to cut heat loss to the soil: high-density extruded polystyrene on blinded, compacted hardcore; a mesh-reinforced slab; a radon barrier.
Such as: the glazed façade facing south, within 30° of the east–west axis; one room deep with no rooms on the sunless north; spacing to avoid overshadowing.

card.stem: “Our common ground starts with the planet. As a species we have never been more vulnerable than we are today. The world is under stress and we are the cause of it. We are now at a tipping point and, as with all periods of great change, there is great opportunity. The world needs the way architects think, we should not keep ourselves aloof from the urgent situation we are in. The most resilient and sustainable form of human habitation is the town or the neighbourhood. We must build to create neighbourhoods. We must plan and design to avoid isolation and disconnection. We must design for what matters, which is ultimately happiness.” Adapted from: PRESIDENT’S INTRODUCTION - Michelle Fagan, President RIAI IRISH ARCHITECTURE, Vol. 3, 2012 / 2013. RIAI, 8 Merrion Square, Dublin 2. ISBN: 978-0-9567493-2-1
